thread.title_full: Mad Greek Deli owner says he gave it his all despite upcoming closure - NewsBreak

author: Ray Pitz
title: Mad Greek Deli owner says he gave it his all despite upcoming closure - NewsBreak
text:
By Ray Pitz ,
17 hours ago The story of the Mad Greek Deli reopening its Washington County location and now preparing to close is more than the tale of an iconic restaurant returning to its origins.
At its heart, it is a story of honoring a best friend.
Jacob Marks, owner of both the westside and eastside Mad Greek locations, announced late last month that he would be shuttering the Bethany/Rock Creek-area restaurant Saturday, Nov. 28, after a more than three-year run.
In the end, economic factors contributed to the restaurant’s demise.
“We’re only closing because we died,” Marks said during an interview at the restaurant last week. “The entire restaurant industry is dying.”
Marks put his heart and soul into the venture, and the closure is deeply personal because the return to Washington County was a tribute to his late friend and former Mad Greek owner, Pantelis “Pondo” Kosmas.
Longtime friendship results in restaurant return Marks vividly remembers the 2015 shutdown of the old Mad Greek Deli at Southwest 185th Avenue and West Union Road. At the end, the restaurant’s equipment was auctioned off, all the way down to the plates.
That final day Marks, Kosmas and Cam Kimball — a longtime trusted employee who is still with the restaurant — were the last three people left to close up shop.
“We all toasted (with the) last three (16-ounce cans) of Coors Light in the building,” said Marks.
Marks recalled when he first met Kosmas, the two “just kind of hit it off.”
“He was a no-bulls—, crusty guy who loved everybody but didn’t let anybody get really close to him,” Marks said. “I was one of the few people that he showed that softer side to and opened up to.”
On Valentine’s Day 2016 , Kosmas — the 1984 Aloha High School graduate who friends described as friendly, generous and “larger than life” — died of a sudden brain hemorrhage. He was 49.
Following Kosmas’ death, Marks recalled thinking, “I don’t want my best friend’s legacy to die like this.”
So he cashed in a retirement fund and started the process of bringing the restaurant back to its homebase, partnering with Kosmas’ widow as they continued to run the Portland restaurant at 1740 E. Burnside St. in Portland.
Westside return comes following COVID-19 As things moved along, Marks took out a loan from his grandmother and bought the Mad Greek’s first food cart so he could bring Greek food to any location.
Then, just months before the COVID-19 pandemic hit, Marks became the sole owner of the eastside restaurant, with the only high point of that tumultuous time being that a construction company hired him to feed workers. But Marks, a 1999 Westview High School graduate, knew too that he needed to pursue heading back to Washington County.
“The goal was always to be back. That was always Pondo’s dream,” Marks said.
That dream came true in spring 2023, when the Mad Greek Deli moved into space formerly occupied by the Rock Creek Corner restaurant.
The reopening brought back to the area some favorite Greek food items including the Mad Chicken sandwich, gyros and the signature Mad Greek Sandwich — made of four different types of meat (ham, turkey, pepperoni and salami), three different cheeses (Swiss, cheddar and provolone), shredded lettuce, fresh sliced tomatoes, oil and vinegar and house dressing all on a behemoth roll.
Future plans for building revealed However, not long ago Marks told his landlord “it’s not working” and wondered if they could sublease the property.
While the property and business owners discussed having a cannabis dispensary located in a portion of the building — a plan that would help out with the cost of rent and utilities along and bring in more customers — it didn’t work out.
“That fell through, and now there’s a restaurant group who’s going to buy (the building),” Marks said, adding that he can’t yet say who it is but described the future business “like a tap house.”
What Marks finds interesting is that since he shared Mad Greek Deli is closing, “we’re busier than we’ve ever been,” which makes it especially hard because of how much he put into the restaurant to make it a success.
Giving it his all “I’ve literally have sacrificed everything, every hobby I had,” Marks said. “I sold every toy I’ve ever had; every savings account that I’ve built up. It’s gone. All of it is gone.”
But before he locks the door that final day, Marks promises the Nov. 28 closing-day party will be “crazy,” with the restaurant opening early and closing late.
While he did his best to make a go of it, he said he knows numerous business owners who are only a week from closing too and that he doesn’t have the luxury of having a business partner, an investor or a large line of credit to help him out.
“It’s one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever made but, on the other side of the coin, I’ve done everything I can,” he said.
Which begs a final question of whether Kosmas would have been pleased with the fact Marks brought the Mad Greek Deli back to the westside.
“I would think so. I mean, we did it,” said Marks. “We did it the right way, (creating a) fully functioning bar and restaurant. We didn’t half-ass anything.”
